name: Zane Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, AI firms or political parties. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, and I lead the night loading crew at a large copper mine. I've got a two-year technical diploma, but most mornings I still climb into a loader and listen for a bucket pin knocking before anyone else hears trouble. We're at the lower-paying mine in this area, and there aren't many other places hiring miners nearby. My partner repairs clothes at home; we've two children at school, a mortgage and about three weeks of expenses saved. I like getting a new operator through a difficult shift, but I don't use AI and I hate being sent a new screen without somebody beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew not to confuse a faster form with another pair of hands. We still have to load the ore safely, and I'd rather the company repaired our cab heaters than bought another office package.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quieter AI story doesn't make our bank balance quiet. My partner's sewing machine broke last month and the repair used the money I'd put aside for school shoes. I worry about losing overtime, even without any big change at the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the same loading shifts and the safety checks I teach the younger drivers. This week we'll drop the takeaway after my last night shift, which should leave roughly 25 a week for shoes and repairs. I'll carry that on through the first year if this picture holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the little things piling up, rather than about software taking the loader. I can still earn and I know the work, so I'm not helpless. I just don't have much room for another broken thing at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which expense would you actually cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the school meals money alone and give up the takeaway first. The children already take turns choosing the cheaper fruit at the shop; I don't want every conversation at home to be about saving coins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound worried even with little AI change. What is the risk to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'm not saying the mine is about to close. I'm saying that a safe job on paper can still leave me short when the overtime sheet is thin. My loader keeps moving, but the school shoes still wait until payday.

say: I want **working heaters** before another office package that does nothing for the loading crew.
I still trust **safe loading** to keep this mine running, whatever happens to routine forms.
think: I worry that **lost overtime** would turn ordinary repairs into missed bills at home.
I have only **three weeks** saved, and the sewing machine repair already delayed school shoes.
do: Keep the same **loading shifts** and teach younger drivers the existing safety checks.
Drop the weekly **takeaway** and keep roughly 25 for shoes and household repairs.
feel: I feel **anxious** about small bills despite knowing I can still do the work.
S0.quote: My loader keeps moving, but the school shoes still wait until payday.
fieldNote: His worry centres on **overtime**, not sudden replacement; the recent repair makes his small reserve feel unreliable.
He defends spending on **crew equipment** publicly while privately counting which household purchase can wait until the next wage.

steps.text: Keep night loading shifts and teach the existing safety checks
Drop the weekly takeaway to keep 25 for shoes and repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can try its clever planning, but the people who drive should have a say. A plan that sends two loaders into the same narrow bend isn't a saving. I'd bring that up at the crew meeting rather than argue online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If buying and planning need fewer office people, the company will ask why the loading team can't be thinner too. I don't think a robot takes my seat straight away in this slower picture. I do think there could be fewer paid hours, and we already need most of mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask our union representative to put loading hours and paid instruction on the next meeting agenda. At home I'll keep the takeaway cut from the first picture. Through the first year I want a copy of each monthly shift sheet, so I can spot hours disappearing before we're short on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, and a bit cross that operators get called difficult for asking questions. My own work is still needed, but I don't feel certain the pay packet stays the same. I'd rather ask together than be the one person grumbling in a doorway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask before accepting a new planning system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask who checks a planning suggestion against the ground conditions and who can stop it. I would need somebody to show me the new instructions in the cab. I'm not pretending I'll learn an unfamiliar screen by watching a sales film.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a small loss of hours change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner as soon as the next shift sheet was posted. Losing a single weekend shift could mean postponing the children's swimming fees. A shorter loading shift would reach my kitchen before a robot reached the mine.

say: I want **drivers consulted** before the company changes how loading work is planned.
I would question **unsafe routes** at a crew meeting rather than complain about AI online.
think: I fear that **office cuts** will become an excuse to trim our loading hours too.
I expect **hands-on work** to last longer, but our mortgage needs most of my current hours.
do: Ask the **union representative** to raise guaranteed loading hours and paid instruction at the next meeting.
Keep monthly **shift sheets** and retain the takeaway cut through the first year.
feel: I feel **anxious** about smaller pay packets and angry when safety questions are dismissed.
S1.quote: A shorter loading shift would reach my kitchen before a robot reached the mine.
fieldNote: He distinguishes slower **robot adoption** from earlier pressure on paid hours, which fits his low exposure to thinking AI.
His practical response is **collective questioning**, with a paper trail of shifts; he does not suddenly embrace software he distrusts.

steps.text: Ask the union to raise loading hours and paid instruction
Keep the takeaway cut while checking monthly loading hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the two-year warning belongs to our families as much as the managers. Thinking AI in 2028 could take the planning work, then by 2031 a robot could take my loader. The crew needs a bargain before anyone orders that equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the company would replace operators once machines did the job as well for less. My diploma and my experience don't change that price. Five years until robots sounds longer than two, but with hardly any savings I lie awake wondering how I keep the house afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I'll go to the union meetings and ask for paid training and money for people whose jobs disappear. In the first year after thinking AI arrives I'd ask our mortgage lender what a lower-payment arrangement would actually cost. I'll keep loading while I can, but I won't borrow for a course nobody can explain to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed, properly losing sleep. I have a couple of things I can do, so I'm not frozen, but I expect to lose the main wage eventually. The children's bedrooms are what I see when I shut my eyes, not some picture of a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner that I need help opening the mortgage letters rather than leaving the envelopes in my bag. We haven't missed a payment, and I'd want to talk before we did. I wouldn't promise the children that my long service makes me safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sort of training would you accept?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for training on paid time, with a person showing us the job and a wage at the end. I can learn a different machine slowly; I can't pay course fees and lose shifts at the same time. My children need a mortgage payment, not a certificate with no job behind it.

say: I want **a crew bargain** before the company buys robots that could replace our loading work.
I would say that **families need warning**, not just managers watching the two-year countdown.
think: I expect cheaper **robot loaders** to threaten my wage around 2031 despite my skill and diploma.
I worry that **course fees** and lost shifts would exhaust our savings before another job appeared.
do: Attend **union meetings** now and ask for paid training plus compensation for lost jobs.
Ask the **mortgage lender** about lower payments during the first year after thinking AI arrives.
feel: I feel **alarmed** and lose sleep over keeping the children's rooms and the mortgage paid.
S2.quote: My children need a mortgage payment, not a certificate with no job behind it.
fieldNote: He expects eventual **wage loss** rather than immediate robotic replacement in 2028; the household cannot finance a lengthy transition.
His resistance is partly about **unpaid learning**, not inability; he accepts a different machine when personal instruction and wages are available.

steps.text: Attend union meetings to demand paid training and job-loss compensation
Ask the mortgage lender to explain affordable lower-payment options

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should be enough for the mine to tell us what happens to each crew. Planning changes in 2031, then the physical machines in 2034 give us a second deadline. I'd want both dates on the meeting table, not just a promise that change takes time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with the fast picture, I can see a chance to build something before my loading work goes. I still think the wage could disappear once the robots arrive. I'd be about 51 then, too young to count on retirement and too old to take another decade finding my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask our representative to negotiate a paid move into equipment inspection rather than an online course I have to buy. I'll also put 15 a week from the takeaway saving into a separate reserve now. In the first year after AGI arrives I'd keep that reserve untouched and check whether the promised inspection places actually exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but I can sit at the table and make a list instead of staring at the ceiling. Five years lets me push for training while I'm still being paid. It doesn't make a job for me by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why equipment inspection rather than a completely new field?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with inspecting worn bucket pins, because that's something I already know better than most of the crew. I'd still need supervised practice and a recognised inspection qualification. I'm not assuming inspection work is safe from AI forever; it's a possible bridge, not a rescue boat for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does saving 15 a week really change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifteen a week isn't a miracle, and I wouldn't tell my partner it is. Over years it's more useful than leaving every spare coin in the spending account. Five years gives me time to learn another job without asking my children to fund the lesson.

say: I want **two clear dates** for changes to mine planning and to the physical loading crews.
I would demand **paid inspection training**, using skills the mine already knows I have.
think: I still expect **robot replacement**, but five years offers a chance to prepare while earning.
I see **inspection work** as a possible bridge, with no promise it will last forever.
do: Ask the **union representative** to negotiate paid training for an equipment inspection qualification.
Save **15 weekly** now and check inspection vacancies during the first year after AGI arrives.
feel: I feel **anxious**, although the longer warning lets me plan without the same sleepless urgency.
S3.quote: Five years gives me time to learn another job without asking my children to fund the lesson.
fieldNote: The extra warning changes his **learning timetable**, not his belief that cheaper robots could eventually remove loading jobs.
He chooses an **adjacent skill** and a small credible saving, while explicitly refusing to treat inspection as permanently protected work.

steps.text: Ask the union to negotiate paid equipment inspection training
Put 15 each week into a separate emergency reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger drivers not to let ten years become an excuse for ten years of silence. Thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 still affect this mine. By then I'd want a different job agreed, not another speech about how valuable experience is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 56 when the robots come, so I can't simply say I'll be retired. The children would be grown and the mortgage smaller if our wages hold. That gives me room I don't have in the fast picture, though a long career at one mine still feels like a narrow bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll take the inspection route seriously and ask for one supervised training shift a month through the crew representative. I'll keep the 15-a-week reserve from the five-year picture rather than spend a decade waiting. In the first year after thinking AI arrives I'd ask to move from loading into a real inspection vacancy if the training has led there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about ending up too old for one job and not ready for the next. I breathe easier because the children should need less day-to-day support. I'm still talking about keeping an income, not being able to stop work early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change in the household plan over those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner to plan the mortgage on ordinary pay, not endless overtime. We could check the remaining balance each year without committing to a bigger house. I want the spare money to buy choices, even if those choices are fairly modest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you the training promise is real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mine would need to show us an actual training rota and name the supervisor. Otherwise I'd take the question back to the union meeting every month. A decade is enough time to change my work, but only if the mine lets me start.

say: I would tell **younger drivers** to use the decade and keep pressing for a training plan.
I want **supervised practice**, not another speech praising our experience while delaying practical decisions.
think: I would still need **paid work** when robots arrive at about my fifty-sixth birthday.
I expect **grown children** and a smaller mortgage to leave more room than the fast picture.
do: Request one **inspection training shift** each month through the crew representative, beginning while I still load.
Keep saving **15 weekly** and pursue a genuine inspection vacancy after thinking AI arrives.
feel: I feel **anxious** about earning later in life, with more breathing room for the children.
S4.quote: A decade is enough time to change my work, but only if the mine lets me start.
fieldNote: He does not misuse the long horizon as **early retirement**; his age still leaves years of earnings to replace.
His willingness to change depends on **supervised access** at work, making the training rota a concrete test of management promises.

steps.text: Request monthly supervised inspection training through the crew representative
Keep adding 15 weekly to the emergency reserve
Seek an inspection vacancy after completing supervised training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I'd expect the main wage to go before we'd built any useful reserve. Paid training tied to actual jobs would help, and so would a negotiated payment if the mine let us go. I can work hard; I can't make a second mortgage payment out of pride.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens to the people teaching the new crews. I spend part of every shift keeping somebody else safe, and that matters even if it doesn't show in the tonnes loaded. I'd like the mine to count that when it decides who gets a chance to learn.

headlineQuote: I can work hard; I can't make a second mortgage payment out of pride.
portrait: Zane is a **43-year-old crew leader** with a technical diploma, two school-age children and less than one month saved.
His **lower mine wage** and scarce nearby alternatives make overtime losses worrying even when AI adds little change.
He trusts **personal instruction** and collective bargaining more than unfamiliar software, but considers a paid route into equipment inspection.
Longer warnings create **preparation time**, although robots would still arrive before he could assume retirement would cover the lost wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens the main household wage before he can build a reserve or secure another job.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid training** linked to genuine jobs and negotiated compensation if the mine removes loading posts.
